findings.title: Denial cache key can collide for different (action, name, parent) tuples
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because dashboard/folder UIDs (name, parent) are allowed to contain underscores, two different tuples can produce the exact same string, e.g. (action="dashboards:read", name="a_b", parent="c") and (action="dashboards:read", name="a", parent="b_c") both yield "...perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_c". Since permDenialCache, permCache, idCache, etc. all share the same underlying cache.Cache instance (only key prefixes differ), this collision causes the cached 'denied' verdict for one resource to be incorrectly applied to a completely different resource/folder combination, producing wrong Check() results for up to the cache TTL.

findings.title: New denial cache can re-introduce the exact bug this PR fixes via a create/permission-grant race
findings.body: After a real (non-cached) permission check returns not-allowed, Check() unconditionally stores a 'deny' entry (s.permDenialCache.Set) keyed by namespace/user/action/name/parent, and this entry is consulted first on every subsequent Check() for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), short-circuiting before any DB lookup. If a user creates a resource and the authorization check races with the commit of the resource's permission grant (the exact scenario this PR intends to fix), the first Check() can observe no permission yet, be denied, and have that denial cached for 30 seconds — meaning the creator would be locked out of their own newly created dashboard/folder for up to 30 seconds even though permission is already correctly granted moments later. Previously (without this denial cache) each subsequent Check() would simply re-evaluate permissions and succeed as soon as the grant was committed.

findings.title: Check() now performs a full permission re-fetch from DB whenever the cached permission map denies a specific resource
findings.body: Previously, getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions checked permCache first and returned the cached scope map unconditionally (whether or not it granted the specific requested resource), so a single cached entry served unlimited Check() calls for any resource until TTL expiry. After this change, that internal cache check was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions; now, whenever getCachedIdentityPermissions finds a cached map but checkPermission against it returns false (resource not found in the cached scope map), Check() falls through and calls getIdentityPermissions again, which unconditionally re-queries permissionStore.GetUserPermissions from the DB. Only the new per-resource permDenialCache prevents repeating this for the exact same resource later. For workflows that call Check() once per resource across many distinct dashboards/folders a user cannot access, each first encounter with a new resource now triggers a full DB permission listing query instead of being resolved for free from the already-valid cached permission map, multiplying DB load compared to before.

findings.title: Denial cache key uses unresolved subject id, inconsistent with other caches
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier parsed directly from the request subject (could be a numeric legacy ID or a UID depending on caller). All other per-user caches (idCache, permCache, teamCache, basicRoleCache) key on the canonical resolved UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers. If the same user is referenced by different subject formats across calls (e.g. numeric ID in one call, UID in another), the denial cache entries will not be shared between them, reducing the cache's effectiveness and making its behavior inconsistent with the rest of the caching scheme.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric conflates two distinct caches and mislabels cache hits
findings.body: The permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented with "true" both when the new permDenialCache short-circuits (line ~118) and when the permission cache actually grants access (line ~132), even though these are two separate caches with different semantics. Additionally, when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached map but checkPermission determines the specific resource is not granted, the code unconditionally records permissionCacheUsage "false" (line 137) even though the permission cache was in fact consulted (just insufficient for this resource). This makes the metric unreliable for distinguishing actual cache-miss rates from 'cache hit but resource not covered' cases, undermining monitoring/alerting based on this metric.

findings.title: No test exercises the write path of the new denial cache
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test manually seeds s.permDenialCache and verifies that Check() reads it, but no test verifies that Check() actually populates permDenialCache after a genuine denial computed from the store (the new write at service.go's s.permDenialCache.Set call). The existing 'should deny user without permission' test in TestService_Check only checks the response value and never asserts that a subsequent call benefits from (or is affected by) the newly written denial cache entry, leaving this core new behavior without direct coverage.
